why: Every cell can only be entered from the cell above or the cell to the left, so best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best[r-1][c], best[r][c-1]). This is the textbook 2-D grid DP the week teaches.
hints: Think about the last move into a cell: it came from above or from the left, nothing else.
best[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(best above, best left); the first row and first column only have one way in.
Fill the table row by row, keeping a single 1-D array of length cols that you overwrite in place. O(rows*cols) time, O(cols) space.
pitfalls: Initialise the first row and column as running sums, not with the min rule (there is no cell above or to the left).
A 1x1 grid answers its single value.
Greedy 'take the cheaper neighbour' fails; you must compare whole path sums.
statement:
You are given a non-empty rectangular grid of non-negative integers. Start at the top-left cell and reach the bottom-right cell. Each step moves exactly one cell right or one cell down.

The sum of a path is the total of every cell on it, including both the start and the end. Return the minimum possible path sum.

Example: grid = [[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]].

  • Path right, right, down, down visits 1, 3, 1, 1, 1: sum 7.
  • Path down, down, right, right visits 1, 1, 4, 2, 1: sum 9.
  • Path down, right, right, down visits 1, 1, 5, 1, 1: sum 9.
  • No path is cheaper than 7, so the answer is 7.
